<!-- Source: README.md -->

# @codenhub/toaster

Toast notifications and native modal dialogs for the browser. Toasts stack in a corner, queue when there are too many, and close on their own. Dialogs ask a question and give you an answer you can `await`. Both are accessible out of the box, both work with a strict Content Security Policy, and neither needs a framework.

> [!WARNING]
>
> This package is experimental. Its API, rendering, and CSS class names may change before a stable release. The [changelog](docs/changelog/index.md) lists every change.

## Installation

```sh
pnpm add @codenhub/toaster
```

## Usage

Load the stylesheet once where your app starts, then call `toast` from anywhere. Dialogs come from their own entry point, so an app that only shows toasts doesn't bundle them:

```ts
import "@codenhub/toaster/styles";
import { toast } from "@codenhub/toaster";
import { dialog } from "@codenhub/toaster/dialog";

toast.success("Note saved");

// A loading spinner that becomes a success or error toast when the promise settles.
const note = await toast.promise(saveNote(draft), {
  loading: "Saving…",
  success: "Saved",
  error: "Save failed",
});

// Resolves to true or false, not to an always-truthy object.
if (await dialog.confirm("Delete this note?", { type: "error", confirmLabel: "Delete" })) {
  await deleteNote(note.id);
}
```

No provider, no setup call: the first toast creates its own stack. For toasts inside a specific element, or separate settings per area, create your own instances with `createToaster()` and `createDialogs()`.

Calls check their input and throw right away on a mistake, such as an empty message or an unknown position. Showing a toast or dialog outside a browser throws too.

## Documentation

- [Documentation overview](docs/index.md): what the package does and the order to read the guides in.
- [Toasts](docs/toasts.md): every kind of toast, actions, promise toasts, updates, queueing, and timers.
- [Dialogs](docs/dialogs.md): `confirm`, `prompt`, `alert`, queueing, and translated labels.
- [Toaster instances](docs/instances.md): every option and default, scoped toasters, `destroy()`, and SSR.
- [Styling](docs/styling.md): colors, presentation classes, dark mode, and CSP.
- [Accessibility and security](docs/accessibility.md): screen readers, focus, reduced motion, and custom content.
- [API reference](docs/reference/index.md): every exported symbol, generated from the source.
- [Changelog](docs/changelog/index.md): what changed in each release.

## Requirements

- A browser. Importing and creating instances is safe during server-side rendering, but showing a toast or dialog needs a `document`.
- `@codenhub/toaster/styles` loaded once. Without it, toasts have no position, layout, or color.
- Native `<dialog>` support for dialogs, which every current browser has.
- Optional: `@codenhub/styles` 0.3.0 or newer. When present, toasts and dialogs take their colors and look from its theme; otherwise built-in colors apply. If you use its native-element stylesheet, import it **before** `@codenhub/toaster/styles`, or dialog buttons lose their colors. See [Styling](docs/styling.md).
- Instances you create own DOM elements, timers, and listeners. Call `destroy()` when the area they belong to goes away.

<!-- Source: docs/index.md -->

# Toaster

Every app eventually needs to say two kinds of things to the person using it. Some news can wait in a corner: "Saved", "Copied", "Sync failed, retrying". Some questions can't: "Delete this note forever?" `@codenhub/toaster` handles both. Toasts are small notifications that stack in a corner of the screen and leave on their own. Dialogs are modal questions that block the page until someone answers.

What it saves you from writing by hand:

- **The stack.** Toasts line up at one of six screen positions. Extra ones wait in a queue, and the oldest one that isn't busy leaves to make room. A toast stays put while someone is hovering over it, has focus inside it, or is waiting on a loading spinner.
- **The timers.** By default, each toast closes after a set time. The countdown pauses while the pointer is on it, while it has focus, and while the browser tab is in the background, so time nobody could spend reading doesn't count.
- **The async dance.** `toast.promise()` shows a spinner while your work runs and turns into a success or error toast when it's done. Dialogs return something you can `await`, so `if (await dialog.confirm("Delete?"))` really is `true` or `false`.
- **The accessibility plumbing.** Screen readers hear every toast, with [one catch while a modal dialog is open](docs/dialogs.md#toasts-while-a-dialog-is-open). Dialogs use the browser's own `<dialog>` element, so focus trapping, <kbd>Escape</kbd>, and returning focus afterward all come from the platform.
- **The security homework.** Strings are always shown as plain text and never parsed as HTML. The package injects no `<style>` element, so a strict Content Security Policy needs no exceptions for it, as long as the stylesheet itself [loads as a file](docs/styling.md#content-security-policy).

It's plain TypeScript working directly with the DOM. There's no framework to adopt and no runtime dependency to install.

## Installation

```sh
pnpm add @codenhub/toaster
```

`npm install`, `yarn add`, and `bun add` work too. The package is ESM only and has two entry points plus a stylesheet:

| Import                     | What you get                                                       |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `@codenhub/toaster`        | `toast`, a ready-made toaster, and `createToaster()` to make more. |
| `@codenhub/toaster/dialog` | `dialog`, a ready-made dialogs instance, and `createDialogs()`.    |
| `@codenhub/toaster/styles` | The stylesheet. Required; nothing looks right without it.          |

Dialogs live in their own entry point so an app that only shows toasts doesn't bundle them. A toast-only bundle costs about 9 KB gzipped.

## A first toast

Load the stylesheet once, in the file where your app starts, then call `toast` anywhere:

```ts
import "@codenhub/toaster/styles";
import { toast } from "@codenhub/toaster";

toast.success("Note saved");
```

That's the whole setup. There's no provider to mount and no container to create. The first toast creates its own stack in `document.body`.

Toaster needs a browser. Importing it during server-side rendering is safe, but showing a toast there throws, because there is no page to put it on. [Toaster instances](docs/instances.md#server-side-rendering) covers how to handle that.

## Reading path

The pages build on each other, and together they follow one small example: a notes app that saves, syncs, renames, and deletes notes. Read them in order the first time.

1. [Toasts](docs/toasts.md): every kind of toast, actions, loading and promise toasts, updating a toast after it's shown, and how stacking, queueing, and timers behave.
2. [Dialogs](docs/dialogs.md): `confirm`, `prompt`, and `alert`, what they resolve to, how they queue, translating their buttons, and what happens to toasts while a dialog is open.
3. [Toaster instances](docs/instances.md): every configuration option and its default, per-kind defaults, scoped toasters for panels and widgets, cleanup with `destroy()`, and server-side rendering.
4. [Styling](docs/styling.md): the stylesheet, colors, presentation classes, dark mode, and Content Security Policy.
5. [Accessibility and security](docs/accessibility.md): what screen readers hear, keyboard and focus behavior, reduced motion, and the trust boundary of custom content.

The [API reference](docs/reference/index.md) lists every exported symbol and signature, generated from the source. The [changelog](docs/changelog/index.md) says what changed in each release.

## Requirements

- A browser with native `<dialog>` support (`HTMLDialogElement.showModal()`) if you use dialogs. Every current browser has it.
- `@codenhub/toaster/styles` loaded once on the page.
- Optional: `@codenhub/styles` 0.3.0 or newer. When it's on the page, toasts and dialogs take their colors and look from its theme. Without it, the package uses its own built-in colors. [Styling](docs/styling.md) explains both.

The package is experimental. Its API, rendering, and CSS class names can still change before a stable release, and the [changelog](docs/changelog/index.md) says what changed each time.

<!-- Source: docs/toasts.md -->

# Toasts

This page covers everything a toast can do: the different kinds, buttons, loading spinners, updating a toast after it appears, where toasts show up, and what happens when too many arrive at once. The examples follow a notes app, starting with the most important feature any notes app has: telling you it saved.

Every example assumes `@codenhub/toaster/styles` is loaded once, as the [overview](docs/index.md#a-first-toast) shows.

## Your first toasts

`toast` is a ready-made toaster. Call it directly for a neutral toast, or use one of its four shortcuts for a toast with a meaning:

```ts
import { toast } from "@codenhub/toaster";

toast("Note saved");
toast.success("Note published");
toast.error("Could not reach the server");
toast.warning("You are offline. Changes will sync later.");
toast.info("A new version is available");
```

`toast()` gives a neutral toast with no icon. The other four each get a matching icon and color, and differ in how urgently screen readers read them out:

| Call              | Read out by screen readers         |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `toast()`         | Politely, after the current speech |
| `toast.success()` | Politely, after the current speech |
| `toast.info()`    | Politely, after the current speech |
| `toast.warning()` | Right away, interrupting           |
| `toast.error()`   | Right away, interrupting           |

Warnings and errors interrupt because they're usually the thing the person needs to hear now. You can change that per toast with `role`; [Accessibility](docs/accessibility.md#what-screen-readers-hear) explains how.

A toast closes itself after 4 seconds. If you'd rather it stayed, read [Timers](#timers-and-auto-dismiss) below.

### Picking the look yourself

The shortcuts are the quick way to give a toast a meaning, but `toast()` takes the same meaning as an option. `type` sets the icon, the color, and how urgently screen readers read it, exactly as the matching shortcut would:

```ts
toast("Storage almost full", { type: "warning" }); // looks and sounds like toast.warning()
toast.success("Note shared", { icon: null }); // a success toast with no icon
toast("Sync paused", { icon: "info" }); // a neutral toast with the info icon
```

`icon` picks one of `"success"`, `"error"`, `"warning"`, `"info"`, or `"loader"`, or `null` for none, whatever the type. The shortcuts always use their own type, so `toast.success("Saved", { type: "error" })` is still a success toast: if the meaning comes from data, call `toast()` with `type`.

### Two ways to call it

`toast()`, `success()`, `error()`, `warning()`, `info()`, and `loading()` all take either a message plus an optional options object, or a single options object:

```ts
toast.success("Note saved", { duration: 6000 });

toast.success({ message: "Note saved", duration: 6000 });
```

They do the same thing. The first reads better for a quick message. The second is handy when the toast is built from data, or when it has a `title` and no `message`.

## Titles, descriptions, and an action button

A toast can hold more than one line. `title` goes on top in bold, `message` is the main text, and `description` sits underneath in smaller print. `action` adds a button:

```ts
import { toast } from "@codenhub/toaster";

toast.success("Moved to trash", {
  title: "Groceries",
  description: "Notes in the trash are deleted after 30 days.",
  action: {
    label: "Undo",
    onClick: (_event, handle) => {
      restoreNote("groceries");
      handle.dismiss();
    },
  },
});
```

`onClick` gets the click's `MouseEvent` and the toast's handle. **Clicking the action does not close the toast.** That's on purpose: some actions should leave it open, like "Show details". When the action is done with the toast, call `handle.dismiss()`, as above.

A toast needs something to say. Calling one with neither a `message` nor a `title` throws `Toast requires a non-empty message or content.` A `description` alone doesn't count: it's the small print, and small print with no headline is just a mystery.

## Loading toasts

Some work takes a while. `toast.loading()` shows a spinner and stays on screen until you change it:

```ts
const syncing = toast.loading("Syncing notes…");
```

A loading toast has no timer and no close button by default, because "still working" shouldn't vanish while the work is still going. To finish it, call `update()` on the handle and turn it into a normal toast:

```ts
import { toast } from "@codenhub/toaster";

const syncing = toast.loading("Syncing notes…");

try {
  const count = await syncNotes();
  syncing.update({
    type: "success",
    message: `${count} notes synced`,
    autoDismiss: true,
  });
} catch {
  syncing.update({
    type: "error",
    message: "Sync failed. Your notes are safe on this device.",
    autoDismiss: true,
  });
}
```

Changing `type` swaps the spinner for the matching icon and color. Leaving the loading state also starts the timer the loading toast never had, with the same settings the matching shortcut, such as `toast.success()`, would get: a `"success"` result closes after the instance's `semantic` duration, or its plain `duration` when the `semantic` group doesn't set one, and stays open if the instance says `autoDismiss: false`. The `autoDismiss: true` above makes this result close either way; pass `autoDismiss: false` instead if it should stay until someone dismisses it. [Per-kind defaults](docs/instances.md#per-kind-defaults) explains the `semantic` group.

`toast.loading()` takes `title`, `message`, `description`, `position`, `dismissible`, `className`, and `margin`. It has no `duration` or `autoDismiss` option, since it never closes on its own; set them in the `update()` that finishes it.

## Promise toasts

That try-and-update pattern is so common it has a shortcut. `toast.promise()` shows a loading toast while a promise runs, then turns it into a success or error toast:

```ts
import { toast } from "@codenhub/toaster";

const note = await toast.promise(saveNote(draft), {
  loading: "Saving…",
  success: (saved) => `Saved "${saved.title}"`,
  error: (error) => `Save failed: ${error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)}`,
});
```

It returns the original promise's result, so `note` is whatever `saveNote()` resolved with. If `saveNote()` rejects, `toast.promise()` shows the error toast and then rejects with the same error, so your own `try`/`catch` still runs. The toast is a side effect; your control flow doesn't change.

The rejection reaches `error` typed as `unknown`, because JavaScript lets a promise reject with anything, not just an `Error`. Check before you read `.message`, as above.

What each option takes:

- **`loading`**: a string, or the same options object `toast.loading()` takes.
- **`success`** and **`error`**: a string, a toast options object, or a function that receives the result (or the error) and returns either one. Return an object when you want a title, description, or action. The result is the loading toast changed in place, so it stays in its stack and gets its type from the outcome: the object takes every toast option except `position`, `margin`, `role`, and `type`.

```ts
await toast.promise(syncNotes(), {
  loading: "Syncing notes…",
  success: (result) => ({
    title: "Sync complete",
    description: `${result.updated} notes updated, ${result.added} added.`,
  }),
  error: () => ({
    message: "Sync failed",
    duration: 10000,
    action: { label: "Retry", onClick: () => syncAgain() },
  }),
});
```

- **`position`**, **`className`**, and **`margin`** apply to the toast the whole way through.
- **`duration`** and **`dismissible`** apply to the result toast. Left unset, they come from the instance's `semantic` defaults, then from the instance itself. [Per-kind defaults](docs/instances.md#per-kind-defaults) explains that chain.

The result toast closes on its own after its `duration`, even though the loading toast before it didn't, unless the instance sets `autoDismiss: false` in its `semantic` group or, when that group leaves it unset, instance-wide. To decide per call, return `autoDismiss` from `success` or `error`; that beats both.

If your `success` or `error` function throws, the loading toast is dismissed and the error is reported to the browser as an uncaught error, so it shows in the console and in error trackers. `toast.promise()` still resolves or rejects with the original promise's outcome, so a typo in a message doesn't break the save.

## Handles: controlling a toast after it appears

Every toast method except `toast.promise()`, which returns the promise's result, returns a `ToastHandle`. Keep it when you want to change, close, or watch the toast later:

```ts
import { toast } from "@codenhub/toaster";

const upload = toast("Uploading attachment… 0%", { autoDismiss: false });

onProgress((percent) => {
  upload.update({ message: `Uploading attachment… ${percent}%` });
});

onDone(() => {
  upload.update({ type: "success", message: "Attachment uploaded", autoDismiss: true });
});

cancelButton.addEventListener("click", () => upload.dismiss());
```

### `update()`

`update()` changes a toast in place. Pass only what you want to change:

- `title`, `message`, `description`: new text, or `null` to remove that line.
- `action`: a new button, or `null` to remove it.
- `type`: `"success"`, `"error"`, `"warning"`, `"info"`, or `"default"`. Changes the color, the icon, and how urgently screen readers announce it.
- `icon`: `"success"`, `"error"`, `"warning"`, `"info"`, or `"loader"` to pick a different icon, or `null` for none. When you change `type` without `icon`, the icon follows the type.
- `content`: replaces everything with custom content, as described in [Custom content](#custom-content). When given, `message` and `icon` in the same call are ignored.
- `duration`, `autoDismiss`, `dismissible`: change timing and the close button. A new `duration` restarts the countdown right away, from the full new value.
- `className`: replaces the classes the toast was called with. The toast's own classes and the toaster's `className` stay, so pass every per-toast class you still want, not just the new one.

Some details that matter in practice:

- **A queued toast keeps its updates.** If the toast is still waiting for room in the stack, the update is stored and applied when it appears.
- **A settled toast ignores updates.** Once the toast has fully closed, `update()` does nothing and doesn't throw. Calling it late is harmless.
- **Focus stays where it was.** If someone has focus on the action button when an update changes only the text, focus stays on the button. If the update replaces the action itself, focus moves to the new button.
- **Changed text is announced again**, so a screen reader hears both "Uploading…" and "Attachment uploaded".
- **A message replaces a lone title.** When a toast has only a `title`, an update with only a `message` takes its place: `toast({ title: "Upload" }).update({ message: "50%" })` shows just "50%". A title-only toast shows its title where the message goes, so a new message takes that spot. Pass `title` in the same update to keep both.

`update()` throws if `duration` isn't a number from 0 to 2147483647, if `type` isn't one of the five above, or if `content` is empty.

### `dismiss()`

`dismiss()` starts the toast's exit animation. It's safe to call more than once, and safe to call on a toast that's still queued, which then never appears.

### State, `settled`, and lifecycle events

A toast moves through four states, readable from `handle.state`:

```text
queued → visible → hiding → hidden
```

- **`queued`**: waiting for room in a full stack. A toast with room skips straight to `visible`.
- **`visible`**: on screen.
- **`hiding`**: playing its exit animation.
- **`hidden`**: gone from the page.

`handle.settled` is a promise that resolves once the toast is `hidden` and its element is removed. Await it when something should happen only after the toast is fully gone.

For finer timing, subscribe to each step. Each method returns a function that unsubscribes:

```ts
const handle = toast("Note archived");

handle.onShow(() => console.log("added to the page"));
handle.onShown(() => console.log("entrance animation finished"));
handle.onHide(() => console.log("exit animation starting"));
const stop = handle.onHidden(() => console.log("removed from the page"));

stop(); // changed our mind about that last one
```

A subscriber added after its step already happened is called right away, so you can't miss an event by subscribing late. If a subscriber throws, the toast still finishes closing, and the error is reported as an uncaught error.

## Positions and margins

Toasts appear at the top right by default. Choose another spot per toast with `position`:

```ts
toast("Copied to clipboard", { position: "bottom-center" });
```

The six positions are `"top-left"`, `"top-center"`, `"top-right"`, `"bottom-left"`, `"bottom-center"`, and `"bottom-right"`. Anything else throws `Invalid toast position: …`. Each position has its own stack. To change the default for every toast, configure the toaster; see [Toaster instances](docs/instances.md#configuration).

`margin` sets the distance from the edge of the screen. It takes one CSS length for both directions, or `x` and `y` separately:

```ts
toast("Saved", { margin: "24px" });
toast("Saved", { margin: { x: "16px", y: "4rem" } });
```

The margin belongs to the stack, not to one toast. Every toast at the same position shares one margin, so the most recent toast that set it moves the whole stack, and a toast that doesn't set it leaves the stack where it is. Without a margin, a stack sits 1rem from the edge, or further when the device has a notch or rounded corners that need more room.

Every toast is 22.25rem (356px) wide, shrinking to fit narrow screens. [Styling](docs/styling.md#size) shows how to change it.

## How the stack fills up

Each position shows at most 5 toasts at once. Set `maxVisible` on the toaster to change that. When a sixth arrives:

1. The new toast joins a first-in, first-out queue.
2. The oldest toast that's allowed to leave starts closing to make room.
3. The queued toast appears in its place.

Some toasts aren't allowed to leave early, because pulling them out from under someone would be rude:

- A toast the pointer is hovering over.
- A toast with keyboard focus inside it, such as on its action button.
- A toast showing the loading spinner. It stands for work that's still running.

If every visible toast is protected, new ones wait in the queue until one of them is released or closes. When a stack is taller than the screen, it scrolls on its own, without showing a scrollbar, so every toast stays reachable.

## Timers and auto-dismiss

A toast closes itself after `duration` milliseconds, 4000 by default:

```ts
toast("Reminder set", { duration: 8000 });
toast("Read this carefully", { autoDismiss: false });
```

`autoDismiss: false` keeps a toast open until it's dismissed. `duration` must be a number from 0 to 2147483647, or the call throws. That ceiling is about 24.8 days, the longest a browser timer can wait; a longer one would fire at once, so a toast meant to stay for a month would vanish on the spot. For "never", `autoDismiss: false` is the honest way to say it.

The countdown pauses while the pointer is over the toast, while focus is inside it, and while the browser tab is in the background. When it resumes, it continues with the time that was left; it doesn't start over. The clock also doesn't start until the entrance animation has finished.

A toast that stays open should have a way out. Set `dismissible: true` to add a close button:

```ts
toast.error("Your note is too long to save", { autoDismiss: false, dismissible: true });
```

## Clearing toasts

```ts
toast.clear(); // closes every toast from this toaster, visible and queued
toast.dismiss(handle); // the same as handle.dismiss()
toast.dismiss(); // the same as toast.clear()
```

These only touch toasts from the same toaster. A [separate instance](docs/instances.md) keeps its own toasts.

## Custom content

When the built-in layout doesn't fit, `toast.custom()` takes your own content. It comes in three forms:

```ts
import { toast } from "@codenhub/toaster";

// 1. A string, shown as plain text.
toast.custom("Week 12 notes exported");

// 2. A DOM node, inserted as is.
const message = document.createElement("p");
const link = document.createElement("a");
link.href = "/trash";
link.textContent = "the trash";
message.append("Deleted. You can still find it in ", link, ".");
toast.custom(message);

// 3. A function that receives the handle and returns a string or a node.
toast.custom((handle) => {
  const button = document.createElement("button");
  button.textContent = "Got it";
  button.addEventListener("click", () => handle.dismiss());
  return button;
});
```

A string is never parsed as HTML: `toast.custom("<b>Hi</b>")` shows the tags as characters. That makes strings safe for text you don't control, such as a note's title. A node goes in exactly as you built it, so its safety is your responsibility. [Accessibility and security](docs/accessibility.md#custom-content-and-trust) explains that boundary.

`toast.custom()` takes `position`, `duration`, `dismissible`, `autoDismiss`, `className`, `role`, and `margin`, either as a second argument or together with `content` in one object. A custom toast has no icon and is announced politely by default.

What custom content can't be:

- An empty or whitespace-only string. It throws `Toast content must not be an empty string.` rather than show an empty box.
- A node other than an element, a text node, or a `DocumentFragment`. Comments and documents throw `Toast content Node must be an Element, Text, or DocumentFragment.`
- A function that returns something other than a string or a node. That throws `Toast content must resolve to a string or DOM Node.`

## When toast calls throw

Toasts check their input when you call them, so a mistake fails right where you made it, not some time later in the browser. Every error is a plain `Error`:

| Message starts with                              | Cause                                                          | Fix                                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Toast requires a non-empty message or content.` | No `message` or `title`, or both are empty.                    | Give the toast some text.                                                       |
| `Toast duration must be a number from 0…`        | `duration` is negative, `NaN`, `Infinity`, or over 2147483647. | Use 0 to 2147483647. For "never", use `autoDismiss: false`.                     |
| `Invalid toast position: …`                      | A position not in the list of six.                             | Use one of the six [positions](#positions-and-margins).                         |
| `Invalid toast role: …`                          | `role` is not `"status"` or `"alert"`.                         | Use one of those two.                                                           |
| `Invalid semantic toast type: …`                 | `type` isn't a known severity.                                 | Use `"success"`, `"error"`, `"warning"`, `"info"`, `"default"`.                 |
| `Toast content …`                                | Empty or unsupported custom content.                           | See [Custom content](#custom-content).                                          |
| `DOM document is not available…`                 | Showing a toast where there's no `document`.                   | Show toasts only in the browser; see [SSR](docs/instances.md#server-side-rendering). |
| `This toaster instance has been destroyed…`      | Calling a toaster after `destroy()`.                           | Create a new one with `createToaster()`.                                        |

## Next

Toasts inform; sometimes you need to ask. [Dialogs](docs/dialogs.md) cover `confirm`, `prompt`, and `alert`, which the notes app uses to ask before deleting a note and to rename one.

<!-- Source: docs/dialogs.md -->

# Dialogs

A toast tells; a dialog asks. Dialogs block the page until someone answers, so they're for the moments that need a decision: "Delete this note?", "What should we call it?", "Your session expired." This page covers the three dialog kinds, what each one resolves to, how they line up when several are opened, translating their buttons, and how they get along with toasts.

Dialogs come from their own entry point, so an app that only shows toasts doesn't pay for them:

```ts
import { dialog } from "@codenhub/toaster/dialog";
```

They use the same stylesheet as toasts, `@codenhub/toaster/styles`.

## Confirm

`dialog.confirm()` asks a yes-or-no question and resolves to a boolean:

```ts
import { dialog } from "@codenhub/toaster/dialog";

if (await dialog.confirm("Delete this note? This can't be undone.")) {
  await deleteNote(note.id);
}
```

It resolves to `true` when the confirm button is pressed and `false` on any way out: the cancel button, <kbd>Escape</kbd>, a click on the backdrop, or `dismiss()`.

Make it clear what's at stake with a title, specific button labels, and `type: "error"`, which colors the confirm button as destructive:

```ts
const confirmed = await dialog.confirm('Delete "Groceries"? This can\'t be undone.', {
  title: "Delete note",
  type: "error",
  confirmLabel: "Delete note",
  cancelLabel: "Keep it",
});
```

"Delete note" and "Keep it" beat "OK" and "Cancel": nobody has ever had to reread a button that says exactly what it does.

## Prompt

`dialog.prompt()` asks for a line of text. It resolves to the text when submitted, or `null` when cancelled:

```ts
import { dialog } from "@codenhub/toaster/dialog";

const name = await dialog.prompt("New name for this note", {
  title: "Rename note",
  defaultValue: note.title,
  placeholder: "Untitled",
  submitLabel: "Rename",
});

if (name !== null && name.trim() !== "") {
  await renameNote(note.id, name.trim());
}
```

The text comes back exactly as typed, spaces included, and may be empty, so check it before you use it. <kbd>Enter</kbd> in the text field submits, unless the person is in the middle of composing a character with an input method editor, as when typing Japanese or Chinese. <kbd>Escape</kbd> cancels. The message is the text field's label, so screen readers announce it with the field.

## Alert

`dialog.alert()` delivers a message that must be acknowledged before anything else happens. It's an accessible replacement for `window.alert()`, and it resolves to `undefined` once closed:

```ts
import { dialog } from "@codenhub/toaster/dialog";

await dialog.alert("Your session has expired. Sign in again to keep editing.", {
  title: "Session expired",
  okLabel: "Sign in",
});

goToSignIn();
```

An alert has one button, but <kbd>Escape</kbd> and the backdrop close it too. All three resolve the same way, because an alert has nothing to decide.

## Dialog options

All three methods take the message first and an options object second:

| Option            | Dialogs             | Default     | What it does                                                                     |
| ----------------- | ------------------- | ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `title`           | All                 | None        | A heading above the message.                                                     |
| `type`            | All                 | `"primary"` | Color of the main button: `"primary"`, `"secondary"`, `"success"`, or `"error"`. |
| `backdropDismiss` | All                 | `true`      | Whether a click on the backdrop closes the dialog as a cancel.                   |
| `className`       | All                 | None        | Extra CSS classes on the `<dialog>` element.                                     |
| `confirmLabel`    | `confirm`           | `"Confirm"` | Text of the confirm button.                                                      |
| `cancelLabel`     | `confirm`, `prompt` | `"Cancel"`  | Text of the cancel button.                                                       |
| `submitLabel`     | `prompt`            | `"Submit"`  | Text of the submit button.                                                       |
| `okLabel`         | `alert`             | `"OK"`      | Text of the only button.                                                         |
| `defaultValue`    | `prompt`            | `""`        | Text already in the field when the dialog opens.                                 |
| `placeholder`     | `prompt`            | None        | Hint shown while the field is empty.                                             |

Set `backdropDismiss: false` when a stray click shouldn't count as an answer, such as in a form someone spent time filling in. <kbd>Escape</kbd> still cancels; that's how the browser's `<dialog>` works, and keyboard users depend on it.

The message must not be empty. An empty or whitespace-only message throws `Interactive dialog message must not be empty.`

## Handles

Each method returns a `DialogHandle`. You can `await` it directly, as every example so far does. You can also keep it and control the dialog while it's open:

```ts
import { dialog } from "@codenhub/toaster/dialog";

const question = dialog.confirm("Discard unsaved changes?");

// Close it if the note gets saved some other way in the meantime.
onAutosave(() => question.dismiss());

const discard = await question;
```

| Member      | What it is                                                                                                                       |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `await`     | The answer: `boolean` for confirm, `string \| null` for prompt, `undefined` for alert.                                           |
| `result`    | The same answer as a real `Promise`, for code that wants one rather than a promise-like value.                                   |
| `dismiss()` | Closes the dialog as a cancel. Works on queued dialogs too. Safe to call more than once.                                         |
| `state`     | `"queued"`, `"visible"`, `"hiding"`, or `"hidden"`, the same states [toasts have](docs/toasts.md#state-settled-and-lifecycle-events). |
| `settled`   | A promise that resolves once the closing animation is done and the dialog is cleaned up.                                         |

The handle being awaitable is the point. Many dialog libraries return an object from `confirm()`, and `if (await confirm(...))` is then always true, because an object is always truthy. That bug ships the "Cancel" button that deletes anyway. Here, `await` gives you the actual answer.

Dismissing gives each kind its cancel value: `false` for confirm, `null` for prompt, `undefined` for alert.

## One at a time

A dialogs instance shows one dialog at a time. Calling `confirm()` while another dialog is open doesn't stack a second dialog on top: the new one waits in a queue, with state `"queued"`, and opens when the current one closes. Dismissing a queued dialog removes it from the queue with its cancel value; it never appears.

When a dialog opens, focus goes to its main button: the confirm button, or the OK button of an `alert()`. A prompt focuses its text field instead, so typing can start right away. A `confirm()` with `type: "error"` focuses the **cancel** button, so a reflexive <kbd>Enter</kbd> on a red "Delete" cancels instead of deleting.

When the last dialog in a sequence closes, focus goes back to the element that had it before the first one opened.

If the browser refuses to open a dialog, which is when `showModal()` throws, that dialog's handle rejects with the browser's error, and the next queued dialog still gets its turn. Wrap the `await` in `try`/`catch` if your page can get into a state where that happens.

## Button labels and translation

Rather than passing labels to every call, set them once on a dialogs instance with `createDialogs()`:

```ts
import { createDialogs } from "@codenhub/toaster/dialog";

const dialogs = createDialogs({
  labels: {
    confirm: "Confirmar",
    cancel: "Cancelar",
    submit: "Enviar",
    ok: "Entendido",
  },
});

if (await dialogs.confirm("¿Borrar esta nota?")) {
  await deleteNote(note.id);
}
```

A label passed to a single call still wins over the instance's label. The toast labels, for the close button and the stack's name, are set on the toaster instead; see [Toaster instances](docs/instances.md#configuration).

## Dialog instances

`createDialogs()` makes an independent instance with the same `confirm`, `prompt`, and `alert` methods as `dialog`, which is itself just an instance made with no options. Each instance has its own queue.

| Option      | Default         | What it does                                                             |
| ----------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `container` | `document.body` | The element the `<dialog>` is added to. Can't be changed after creation. |
| `labels`    | English         | Default button labels: `confirm`, `cancel`, `submit`, `ok`.              |
| `className` | None            | Extra CSS classes on every dialog from this instance.                    |

`configure()` changes `labels` and `className` later. New labels apply to dialogs called afterwards; a dialog already waiting in the queue keeps the labels it was called with. A new `className` applies to every dialog that opens afterwards, queued ones included. Passing `container` to it throws `Dialogs container cannot be changed after construction.`

`destroy()` closes the open dialog and drops the queued ones, resolving each with its cancel value, and removes the instance's `<dialog>` element. Calling it twice does nothing. Any other call after it throws `This dialogs instance has been destroyed. Create a new one with createDialogs().`

Opening a dialog outside a browser throws `DOM document is not available. Dialogs require a browser environment.` Like toasts, dialogs are safe to import during server-side rendering, just not to open.

## Toasts while a dialog is open

A modal dialog makes the rest of the page inert: nothing behind it can be clicked, focused, or heard by a screen reader. A toast stuck behind the backdrop would be useless, so while a dialog from this package is open, the toasts move into it.

More precisely: every toaster that renders into the same element as the dialog moves its stacks and its screen reader announcements inside the open dialog. Toasts stay in their usual corner, above the backdrop, and remain clickable and announced. They move back as soon as the dialog starts closing. With dialogs opened inside dialogs, the toasts follow the most recent one.

```ts
const deleting = dialog.confirm("Delete this note?");
toast.info("Autosave paused"); // shown above the backdrop, still clickable
```

Toasters with a different container, such as one scoped to a sidebar, don't move. Their toasts stay behind the backdrop, inert and not announced, until the dialog closes, and they aren't announced again afterward.

### Your own modal dialogs

This only works with dialogs from this package. A `<dialog>` your app opens with `showModal()` makes the page inert too, and the package won't move toasts into it. Toasts shown while it's open render behind its backdrop, where nobody can click them and screen readers skip them.

The fix is a toaster that lives inside your dialog. Create it each time the dialog opens and destroy it when it closes, since a destroyed toaster can't be reused:

```ts
import { createToaster } from "@codenhub/toaster";

const settings = document.querySelector<HTMLDialogElement>("#settings")!;

function openSettings() {
  const settingsToaster = createToaster({ container: settings });
  settings.addEventListener("close", () => settingsToaster.destroy(), { once: true });
  settings.showModal();
  return settingsToaster;
}

const settingsToaster = openSettings();
settingsToaster.success("Preferences saved");
```

## Next

The notes app now has toasts and dialogs from the ready-made instances. [Toaster instances](docs/instances.md) covers every configuration option, defaults per toast kind, and separate toasters like the one above.

<!-- Source: docs/instances.md -->

# Toaster instances

So far everything went through `toast`, the ready-made toaster. This page is about making your own with `createToaster()`, and about the options both kinds share: where toasts appear, how long they stay, how many fit, and what their built-in labels say. It also covers cleaning up, which matters the moment a toaster lives inside something that can disappear, and server-side rendering.

## When you need your own

Most apps never need more than `toast`, configured once. Create a separate toaster when:

- Toasts belong inside a specific element, such as a side panel, an embedded widget, or [your own modal dialog](docs/dialogs.md#your-own-modal-dialogs), rather than over the whole page.
- You're building a widget that gets embedded in pages you don't control, and its toasts shouldn't mix with the host page's.
- You want a fresh toaster per test, so one test's leftover toasts can't fail the next.

A container decides where the stacks live in the page, not where they're drawn. Stacks are `position: fixed`, so they still sit at the edges of the viewport, unless the container is a containing block for fixed elements, as one with `transform` or `contain: layout` is. Inside a dialog that's exactly what you want; for a side panel, add `contain: layout` to the panel so the corners are the panel's.

For different settings in different parts of one page, per-call options on `toast` are usually enough. More toasters mean more stacks, and [two toasters in the same corner](#instances-are-independent) end up on top of each other.

## Configuration

`createToaster()` takes an optional configuration object. Every field is optional:

```ts
import { createToaster } from "@codenhub/toaster";

const sidebarToaster = createToaster({
  container: document.querySelector<HTMLElement>("#sidebar")!,
  position: "bottom-left",
  maxVisible: 3,
  duration: 6000,
  dismissible: true,
  labels: { dismiss: "Close notification" },
});

sidebarToaster.success("Folder created");
```

| Option        | Default                         | What it does                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------- | ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `container`   | `document.body`                 | The element the toast stacks are added to. Can't be changed later.                                                                                   |
| `position`    | `"top-right"`                   | Where toasts appear when a call doesn't say. One of the six [positions](docs/toasts.md#positions-and-margins).                                            |
| `maxVisible`  | `5`                             | How many toasts each position shows at once before the rest [queue](docs/toasts.md#how-the-stack-fills-up). A whole number of 1 or more.                  |
| `duration`    | `4000`                          | Milliseconds before a toast closes itself. From 0 to 2147483647.                                                                                     |
| `autoDismiss` | `true`                          | Whether toasts close themselves after `duration`.                                                                                                    |
| `dismissible` | `false`                         | Whether toasts get a close button.                                                                                                                   |
| `margin`      | 1rem, or the device's safe area | Distance from the edge, as a CSS length or `{ x, y }`. See [margins](docs/toasts.md#positions-and-margins).                                               |
| `className`   | None                            | Extra CSS classes on every toast from this toaster.                                                                                                  |
| `labels`      | English                         | `dismiss`, the close button's accessible name (`"Dismiss toast"`), and `notifications`, the name screen readers give each stack (`"Notifications"`). |
| `semantic`    | None                            | Defaults for `success`, `error`, `warning`, `info`, and `promise` results. See [Per-kind defaults](#per-kind-defaults).                              |
| `loading`     | None                            | Defaults for `loading` toasts and the loading part of `promise`.                                                                                     |
| `custom`      | None                            | Defaults for `custom` toasts.                                                                                                                        |

The `toast` you import is a toaster created with no options, so these defaults are exactly how it behaves until you `configure()` it.

`createToaster()` copies the configuration. Changing the object you passed in afterwards does nothing; use `configure()` for that.

Bad values throw right away, when the toaster is created:

- `Toaster duration must be a number from 0 to 2147483647.`
- `Toaster maxVisible must be a positive integer.` A `maxVisible` of 0, 2.5, or -1 all throw.
- `Toaster nested duration must be a number from 0 to 2147483647.` The same rule for `semantic.duration` and `custom.duration`.
- `Invalid toast position: …` For `position` or any per-kind `position`.

## Per-kind defaults

Sometimes one kind of toast needs different defaults. Errors, for example, often deserve more reading time and a close button, because nobody reads an error message in under 4 seconds, least of all the one about losing their work:

```ts
import { createToaster } from "@codenhub/toaster";

const notesToaster = createToaster({
  duration: 4000,
  semantic: { duration: 8000, dismissible: true },
  loading: { position: "bottom-right" },
  custom: { autoDismiss: false },
});
```

| Group      | Applies to                                                         | Fields                                                                   |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `semantic` | `success`, `error`, `warning`, `info`, and the result of `promise` | `position` (not for `promise`), `duration`, `dismissible`, `autoDismiss` |
| `loading`  | `loading` and the loading part of `promise`                        | `position`, `dismissible`                                                |
| `custom`   | `custom`                                                           | `position`, `duration`, `dismissible`, `autoDismiss`                     |

A plain `toast()` call uses only the instance-wide settings. For every other kind, each setting is looked up in this order, and the first one that's set wins:

1. The option passed to the call itself.
2. The matching per-kind group.
3. The instance-wide setting.
4. The built-in default.

With the configuration above, `notesToaster.error("Sync failed")` stays for 8 seconds with a close button, `notesToaster("Saved")` stays for 4, and `notesToaster.error("Sync failed", { duration: 2000 })` stays for 2. An option set to `undefined` in a call counts as not set, so it doesn't erase the per-kind default.

The result of `promise` bends these rules for position, because it's the loading toast updated in place rather than a new toast. Its position never changes, so it's wherever the loading toast went: the `loading` options object, then the call's `position`, then the `loading` group, then the instance. `semantic.position` never applies.

## Changing settings later

`configure()` changes any option except `container`. Pass only what changes:

```ts
import { toast } from "@codenhub/toaster";

toast.configure({
  position: "bottom-center",
  labels: { dismiss: "Fechar", notifications: "Notificações" },
});
```

Most changes apply to toasts shown afterwards. Three apply right away to toasts already on screen:

- **`maxVisible`**: lowering it closes the oldest toasts beyond the new limit straight away, except [protected ones](docs/toasts.md#how-the-stack-fills-up), which leave when they're released.
- **`margin`**: existing stacks move.
- **`labels.notifications`**: existing stacks are renamed.

An option passed as `undefined` goes back to its default, the same as leaving it out of `createToaster()`, and that reaches the screen too: `configure({ margin: undefined })` puts existing stacks back at the default margin, and `configure({ maxVisible: undefined })` lets 5 show again. So `configure({ margin: compact ? "8px" : undefined })` does what it reads like.

`configure()` validates like `createToaster()` does and throws the same errors. Passing `container` throws `Toaster container cannot be changed after construction.` To move toasts somewhere else, create a new toaster there and destroy the old one.

## Cleaning up with `destroy()`

A toaster adds elements, timers, and event listeners to the page. When the thing it belongs to goes away, such as a sidebar closing or a widget unmounting, call `destroy()`:

```ts
import { createToaster } from "@codenhub/toaster";

function mountSidebar(sidebar: HTMLElement) {
  const sidebarToaster = createToaster({ container: sidebar });

  // … use sidebarToaster while the sidebar is open …

  return function unmountSidebar() {
    sidebarToaster.destroy();
  };
}
```

`destroy()` works immediately, with no animations:

1. Every toast, visible or queued, closes at once. Their state becomes `"hidden"` and their `settled` promises resolve.
2. The toaster's stacks and screen reader regions are removed from the page.
3. Its timers and listeners are removed.
4. Every later call on it, except another `destroy()`, throws `This toaster instance has been destroyed. Create a new one with createToaster().`

Calling `destroy()` again does nothing, so it's safe in cleanup code that might run twice. Destroying a toaster doesn't affect any dialogs instance, and destroying a dialogs instance doesn't affect toasters.

You can destroy the ready-made `toast` too, but there's no way to get it back afterwards. Leave it alone unless the whole app is shutting down.

## Instances are independent

Two toasters never coordinate. Each one has its own stacks, its own queue, and its own `maxVisible`, even at the same position:

```ts
const first = createToaster({ position: "top-right" });
const second = createToaster({ position: "top-right" });

first.success("From the first toaster");
second.success("From the second toaster"); // drawn on top of the first one
```

Both stacks sit in the same corner and overlap. Give separate toasters separate positions or containers, or use one toaster with per-call options.

## Server-side rendering

Toaster can be imported anywhere. Creating a toaster, including the ready-made `toast`, doesn't touch the page, so it's safe while rendering on the server. So is `configure()`: without a page it stores the settings, and they apply once toasts render in the browser. Showing something needs a page, so a toast or dialog call made where there's no `document` throws:

- `DOM document is not available. Toaster operations require a browser environment.`
- `DOM document is not available. Dialogs require a browser environment.`

In Next.js, Remix, SvelteKit, Astro, and similar frameworks, show toasts from code that only runs in the browser: event handlers, effects (`useEffect`, `onMount`), or client-only modules:

```tsx
"use client";

import { toast } from "@codenhub/toaster";

export function SaveButton({ onSave }: { onSave: () => Promise<void> }) {
  async function save() {
    try {
      await toast.promise(onSave(), { loading: "Saving…", success: "Saved", error: "Save failed" });
    } catch {
      // toast.promise() already showed the error toast.
    }
  }

  return <button onClick={save}>Save</button>;
}
```

## Next

The notes app has all the toasts and dialogs it needs. Time to make them look like they belong: [Styling](docs/styling.md) covers colors, presentation, size, dark mode, and Content Security Policy.

<!-- Source: docs/styling.md -->

# Styling

Toasts and dialogs should look like part of your app, not like a library that wandered in. This page covers the stylesheet, where the colors come from, the presentation classes, size, dark mode, overriding colors yourself, and Content Security Policy. Everything here is plain CSS: no build plugin, no theme object, no runtime styling API.

## The stylesheet

Load the stylesheet once, where your app starts:

```ts
import "@codenhub/toaster/styles";
```

It holds everything visual: the stacks and their positions, toast and dialog layout, animations, and colors. Without it, toasts are still added to the page, but with no positioning, layout, or color. If your first toast shows up looking like a forgotten paragraph at the bottom of the page, this import is the reason.

The import works with any bundler that handles CSS imports, such as Vite, webpack, or esbuild. Without a bundler, link `dist/styles/index.css` from the package with a `<link rel="stylesheet">` tag.

### What it sets outside toasts

Almost every rule is scoped to the package's own elements, but a few are page-wide, and it's better to hear about them here than from a confused teammate:

- **`color-scheme` on the root.** The stylesheet sets `color-scheme: light dark` on `:root`, so the browser draws built-in controls such as scrollbars and form fields in dark mode when the operating system prefers dark. The `dark`, `light`, `theme-dark`, and `theme-light` classes and the `data-theme` attribute set it too, on whatever element carries them; see [Dark mode](#dark-mode). If your page sets its own `color-scheme`, yours applies wherever your rule is more specific or loads later.

  The rule is there because the built-in colors are `light-dark()` pairs, which follow `color-scheme`: without it, standalone toasts would stay light on a dark system. If your page only has a light design, the side effect is dark scrollbars and form fields for visitors whose system prefers dark. Opt out with the `light` class on `<html>`, or with your own rule, loaded after this stylesheet and outside any `@layer`, since the toaster's rule isn't in one either:

  ```css
  :root {
    color-scheme: light;
  }
  ```

  Toasts follow along and stay light too, so nothing on the page changes theme behind your back.

- **Presentation classes.** It defines `.solid`, `.soft`, `.ghost`, `.edged`, and `.edgeless` globally, in the CSS `@layer components`. They only set the `--ui-fill`, `--ui-fg-on-fill`, and `--ui-border` custom properties. An element of your own that happens to share a class name won't change by itself, but those properties are inherited, and toasts and `@codenhub/styles` components read them, so anything of that kind inside it picks them up. If `.solid` already means something else in your app, rename yours.

## Where the colors come from

Toasts and dialogs pick their colors in one of two ways, depending on whether `@codenhub/styles` is on the page.

### Standalone

Without `@codenhub/styles`, the stylesheet uses built-in colors: a neutral surface for default toasts, green for success, red for error, amber for warning, and blue for info, each with a light and a dark version. You don't need to set anything up.

### With `@codenhub/styles`

[`@codenhub/styles`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@codenhub/styles) is an optional design system. When its stylesheet, version 0.3.0 or newer, is on the page, toasts and dialogs build their colors from its theme instead:

- **Intent colors**: toasts read `--color-success`, `--color-destructive` (for errors), `--color-warning`, and `--color-info`, and dialog buttons read `--color-primary`, `--color-accent` (for `type: "secondary"`), `--color-success`, and `--color-destructive`, so changing your theme's colors changes both.
- **Presentation**: how much color fills the background and the border follows `--ui-fill` and `--ui-border`.
- **Look and feel**: a theme's corner radius, border width, shadow, clipping, and elevation (`--ui-radius`, `--ui-border-width`, `--ui-surface-shadow`, `--ui-clip`, `--ui-elevation`) apply to toasts and dialogs too, so a glassy or neobrutalist theme reaches them as well.

These are read live. Change a theme variable or class at runtime and toasts already on screen update with it.

By default a toast looks like a `@codenhub/styles` alert: a lightly tinted surface with a border and no shadow. Dialog buttons look like its buttons: solid color, no border, slightly raised.

## Presentation classes

Pass a presentation class through `className` to change how strongly a toast is colored:

| Class      | Effect                                    |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `solid`    | Fully colored background.                 |
| `soft`     | Lightly tinted background. Toast default. |
| `ghost`    | No background fill.                       |
| `edged`    | Draws the border. Toast default.          |
| `edgeless` | Removes the border.                       |

```ts
import { toast } from "@codenhub/toaster";

toast.error("Note could not be saved", { className: "solid" });
toast.info("Syncing in the background", { className: "ghost edgeless" });
```

These classes work standalone and with `@codenhub/styles`. They set `--ui-fill` and `--ui-border`, so a class on the toast itself beats one on any ancestor. To apply one to every toast from a toaster, use the toaster's `className` option.

## Size

Every toast is 22.25rem (356px) wide. On a narrow screen it shrinks to fit, keeping the stack's margin on both sides. All toasts in a stack share the same width, so the stack keeps straight edges.

To change the width, set `width` in a class and pass it through `className`:

```css
.wide-toast {
  width: 28rem;
}
```

```ts
toast.info("A longer message that needs more room", { className: "wide-toast" });
```

## Animation speed

Toasts slide in and out over 400ms, and dialogs fade over 200ms. Both read the same motion custom properties `@codenhub/styles` uses, so you can change them with or without it:

| Property                   | Default                      | Controls                                      |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `--motion-duration-slow`   | `400ms`                      | Toast entrance, exit, and sliding in a stack. |
| `--motion-ease`            | `cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1)` | Easing of those toast animations.             |
| `--motion-duration-normal` | `200ms`                      | Dialog and backdrop fades.                    |

```css
:root {
  --motion-duration-slow: 250ms;
}
```

Reduced motion turns all of these off regardless; see [Reduced motion](docs/accessibility.md#reduced-motion).

## Dark mode

With no theme set, toasts and dialogs follow the operating system's light or dark preference. To choose explicitly, put one of these on an ancestor, usually `<html>`:

- Dark: the `dark` or `theme-dark` class, or `data-theme="dark"`.
- Light: the `light` or `theme-light` class, or `data-theme="light"`.

`@codenhub/theme` sets the `theme-<name>` class and `data-theme="<name>"`, so themes named `dark` and `light` match out of the box. For dark themes with other names, turn on its `darkClass` option, which adds the `dark` class.

Colors are resolved with CSS `light-dark()` against each element's own `color-scheme`, so a light section inside a dark page works. Toasts rendered inside it, by a [toaster scoped to that section](docs/instances.md), use light colors:

```html
<html class="dark">
  <body>
    <aside id="preview" class="light" style="color-scheme: light">
      <!-- A toaster created with { container: preview } shows light toasts here. -->
    </aside>
  </body>
</html>
```

## Color overrides

When a color has to differ from the theme, set the matching `--toast-color-*` custom property in your own CSS. It replaces the computed color for that one value, standalone or with `@codenhub/styles`. Each value is final: it's used exactly as given, not mixed with anything.

Custom properties are inherited, so where you set one decides what it affects:

```css
/* Every toast and dialog on the page. */
:root {
  --toast-color-success-bg: #0f2e1b;
  --toast-color-success-fg: #4ade80;
  --toast-color-success-edge: #166534;
}

/* Only toasts inside the sidebar, from a toaster created with { container: sidebar }. */
#sidebar {
  --toast-color-error-bg: #450a0a;
  --toast-color-error-fg: #fca5a5;
}

/* One toast, through className. */
.quota-alert {
  --toast-color-error-bg: #7f1d1d;
}
```

```ts
toast.error("Storage almost full", { className: "quota-alert" });
```

For dialogs, put the class on the dialog with the call's `className` or the instance's `className`.

| Property                     | What it colors                                                                          |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--toast-color-default-bg`   | Background of a neutral toast.                                                          |
| `--toast-color-default-fg`   | Text and icon of a neutral toast.                                                       |
| `--toast-color-default-edge` | Border of a neutral toast.                                                              |
| `--toast-color-success-bg`   | Background of a success toast.                                                          |
| `--toast-color-success-fg`   | Text and icon of a success toast.                                                       |
| `--toast-color-success-edge` | Border of a success toast.                                                              |
| `--toast-color-error-bg`     | Background of an error toast.                                                           |
| `--toast-color-error-fg`     | Text and icon of an error toast.                                                        |
| `--toast-color-error-edge`   | Border of an error toast.                                                               |
| `--toast-color-warning-bg`   | Background of a warning toast.                                                          |
| `--toast-color-warning-fg`   | Text and icon of a warning toast.                                                       |
| `--toast-color-warning-edge` | Border of a warning toast.                                                              |
| `--toast-color-info-bg`      | Background of an info toast.                                                            |
| `--toast-color-info-fg`      | Text and icon of an info toast.                                                         |
| `--toast-color-info-edge`    | Border of an info toast.                                                                |
| `--toast-color-surface`      | Background of a dialog and its cancel button.                                           |
| `--toast-color-text`         | Text of a dialog and its cancel button.                                                 |
| `--toast-color-border`       | Border of a dialog and its cancel button under `edged`, and of the prompt's text field. |
| `--toast-color-primary-bg`   | Focus ring and focused border of the prompt's text field.                               |

The package never sets these properties itself. They're entirely yours.

## Content Security Policy

The package injects no `<style>` element. The stylesheet is one you load, and the only styles the package writes are individual properties on elements through `element.style.setProperty()`, which a `style-src` policy doesn't block. A strict policy such as this one needs no nonce or exception for it:

```http
Content-Security-Policy: style-src 'self';
```

That covers the package. How you load the stylesheet is between you and your policy: a `<link>` or a CSS file your bundler emits is fine under `style-src 'self'`, but some setups, such as dev servers or `style-loader`, inject CSS as a `<style>` element, which this policy blocks. If toasts show up unstyled under CSP, check that first.

The package also never parses HTML, so it works under Trusted Types as well; see [Accessibility and security](docs/accessibility.md#trusted-types).

## Stylesheet order with `@codenhub/styles/native`

If you use `@codenhub/styles`' native-element stylesheet (`@codenhub/styles/native` or `@codenhub/styles/tw/native`), import it **before** the toaster stylesheet:

```ts
import "@codenhub/styles/native";
import "@codenhub/toaster/styles";
```

The native stylesheet styles every plain `<button>` as a neutral button. Dialog buttons are plain `<button>` elements, and both stylesheets style them with equally weak selectors, so whichever loads last wins. Load the native stylesheet last and every dialog button turns neutral, including the red "Delete" one, which is exactly the button that most needs to look dangerous.

## Next

The notes app looks the part. The last page, [Accessibility and security](docs/accessibility.md), covers what screen reader users hear, how focus moves, reduced motion, and the trust boundary of custom content.

<!-- Source: docs/accessibility.md -->

# Accessibility and security

A toast that only some people can perceive is a toast that only some people get. This page covers what the package does for screen reader and keyboard users without being asked, the few things it leaves to you, and the security line between text and DOM nodes in custom content.

## What screen readers hear

Every toast is announced. Each toaster adds two hidden "live regions" to its container: elements whose changing text screen readers read out automatically. One is polite, the other assertive. A toast's `role` picks which one reads it:

- **`"status"`** is polite: read after whatever the screen reader is currently saying. It's the default for `toast()`, `success()`, `info()`, `loading()`, and `custom()`.
- **`"alert"`** is assertive: read right away, interrupting. It's the default for `error()` and `warning()`.

Change it per toast when the default doesn't fit:

```ts
import { toast } from "@codenhub/toaster";

// A routine warning that doesn't need to interrupt anyone.
toast.warning("Note is getting long", { role: "status" });
```

Any other `role` value throws `Invalid toast role: …`.

What gets read:

- The toast's title, message, and description, or the text inside custom content.
- The action button's label, after the text, as in "Moved to trash. Undo", so the listener knows there's something to act on.
- Not the close button, and not buttons inside custom content.

A toast is announced again whenever an update changes its text or role. That's how a promise toast announces both "Saving…" and "Saved".

Two timing details explain behavior you might notice while testing:

- **The first announcement is slightly delayed.** Screen readers often miss a live region that appears with its text already in it, because they only announce changes to regions they're already watching. So each region is added empty, and its first text arrives 100ms later, following the [W3C ARIA22 technique](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Techniques/aria/ARIA22.html).
- **Announced text is cleared after 7 seconds**, so the hidden regions don't pile up old messages.

The visible toast itself isn't a live region and has no `role` attribute. Tests that find toasts by `role="status"` or `aria-live` need another selector. Find them the way a screen reader user does, through the stack's landmark, described next:

```ts
// Playwright; Testing Library's getByRole works the same way.
const notifications = page.getByRole("region", { name: "Notifications" }); // or your labels.notifications
await expect(notifications.getByText("Note saved")).toBeVisible();
```

### Finding the toasts

Each stack is a landmark region named "Notifications". Screen reader users can jump to it from their landmarks list to reach a toast's buttons. A stack with no toasts leaves the list, so nobody lands in an empty region. Translate the name with the toaster's `labels`:

```ts
import { createToaster } from "@codenhub/toaster";

const toaster = createToaster({
  labels: {
    notifications: "Notificações",
    dismiss: "Fechar notificação",
  },
});
```

`dismiss` is the accessible name of the close button on [dismissible](docs/toasts.md#timers-and-auto-dismiss) toasts. It defaults to "Dismiss toast".

### Toasts under a dialog

While a dialog from this package is open, toasts from toasters sharing its container are announced from inside the dialog. Toasts from other toasters, and toasts shown under a modal dialog your app opened itself, aren't announced at all, and aren't announced later either. [Toasts while a dialog is open](docs/dialogs.md#toasts-while-a-dialog-is-open) explains why and how to avoid it.

## Keyboard and focus

Toasts never steal focus. Showing one doesn't move the keyboard anywhere, which is what you want for something that's supposed to stay out of the way.

When someone does move focus into a toast, such as by tabbing to its action button:

- Its timer pauses, and it's [protected from being pushed out](docs/toasts.md#how-the-stack-fills-up) of a full stack.
- If an update changes only its text, focus stays on the button. If the update replaces the action, focus moves to the new button.
- When it closes, focus goes back to whatever had focus when the toast appeared, as long as that element is still on the page. If focus has already moved somewhere else in the meantime, it stays there.

Dialogs use the browser's native `<dialog>` element with `showModal()`, so the browser itself handles:

- **Hiding the rest of the page.** Everything behind the dialog is inert: no clicks, no focus, and screen readers skip it.
- **Keeping focus inside.** <kbd>Tab</kbd> cycles through the dialog's own controls.
- **<kbd>Escape</kbd>**, which cancels.
- **Returning focus.** When the last dialog in a [queue](docs/dialogs.md#one-at-a-time) closes, focus goes back to the element that had it before the first one opened.

The title and message are linked to the dialog as its accessible name and description, and a prompt's message labels its text field.

## Reduced motion

Some people turn on reduced motion in their operating system, because sliding and fading can cause dizziness or nausea. When `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` is on:

- Toasts appear and disappear without animating.
- Toasts in a stack jump to their new position instead of sliding.
- Dialog backdrops appear and disappear without fading.

Nothing to configure. The setting is read live, so changing it while the page is open takes effect for the next animation.

## What's left to you

The package handles the mechanics, but some choices only you can make:

- **Time to read.** A toast that closes after 4 seconds is fine for "Saved" and too fast for anything someone has to act on or read twice. Give important toasts a longer `duration`, or `autoDismiss: false` with `dismissible: true`. Better still, don't put anything a person must not miss only in a toast.
- **Labels in other languages.** The built-in labels are English. Set the toaster's `labels` and the dialogs' `labels`, as [Dialogs](docs/dialogs.md#button-labels-and-translation) shows.
- **Custom content.** Nodes you pass to `toast.custom()` are yours: give buttons and links accessible names, keep the reading order sensible, and keep interactive elements keyboard-reachable.
- **Color overrides.** Colors you set with `--toast-color-*` need enough contrast against each other. The built-in colors are designed for it; your overrides are on you.

## Custom content and trust

`toast.custom()` and the `content` option of `update()` accept a string or a DOM node, and the two are treated very differently:

| You pass   | What happens                                               | Safe for untrusted input?    |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| A string   | Shown as plain text. Never parsed as HTML.                 | Yes.                         |
| A node     | Inserted exactly as built.                                 | Only if you built it safely. |
| A function | Called with the handle; its result follows the rows above. | Depends on what it returns.  |

### Strings are text

A string becomes a single text node. Tags in it show up as characters and create no elements:

```ts
import { toast } from "@codenhub/toaster";

// Shows the characters <b>Groceries</b>, not bold text.
toast.custom("<b>Groceries</b>");
```

That makes strings safe for anything users or servers control, such as note titles, user names, and error messages from an API. The same goes for every other text option: `message`, `title`, `description`, action labels, and dialog text are all inserted as text.

### Nodes are trusted

A node is inserted as is. The package doesn't inspect or clean it, so whoever builds it is responsible for its safety. Build it with DOM methods and put untrusted text in through `textContent`, never through `innerHTML`:

```ts
import { toast } from "@codenhub/toaster";

toast.custom((handle) => {
  const wrapper = document.createElement("div");

  const text = document.createElement("span");
  text.textContent = `Shared "${note.title}" with ${recipient.name}`;

  const button = document.createElement("button");
  button.textContent = "Copy link";
  button.addEventListener("click", () => {
    copyShareLink(note.id);
    handle.dismiss();
  });

  wrapper.append(text, button);
  return wrapper;
});
```

Event listeners you attach to your own nodes are yours to manage. They're released with the node when nothing else references it, but anything they hold onto elsewhere, such as a subscription or a timer, needs your own cleanup, for example in `handle.onHidden()`.

### Trusted Types

The package never assigns to `innerHTML` or any other HTML-parsing property. Its own toasts, icons, and dialogs are built with DOM methods. A page enforcing Trusted Types with `require-trusted-types-for 'script'` needs no Trusted Types policy for it. Its styling is CSP-friendly too; see [Content Security Policy](docs/styling.md#content-security-policy).

## Next

That's the whole tour. For exact signatures and types, see the [API reference](docs/reference/index.md). To see what changed between versions, see the [changelog](docs/changelog/index.md). To start over from the top, head back to the [overview](docs/index.md).

<!-- Source: docs/changelog/0.4.0.md -->

# 0.4.0

## Added

- `@codenhub/toaster/dialog` exports `dialog` and `createDialogs`. While one of its dialogs is open, the toasts of every toaster rendering into the same parent move into it, as before.

## Changed

- Dialogs are no longer part of `@codenhub/toaster`, so an app that only shows toasts no longer bundles them: `toast("…")` alone costs about 9.1 KB gzipped, down from 12.7 KB. `dialog` and `toaster.dialog` are gone from the main entry; import `dialog` or `createDialogs` from `@codenhub/toaster/dialog`. The `confirm`, `cancel`, `submit`, and `ok` labels move to `DialogsConfig.labels`, a toaster's `className` and `destroy()` no longer affect dialogs, and `DialogDispatcher` is renamed `Dialogs`.
- String content passed to `toast.custom()`, the `content` option, or `update({ content })` renders as plain text, so markup in it shows literally. Pass a DOM node or a node factory for formatted content. The package no longer uses any HTML-parsing sink, so a Trusted Types policy needs nothing for it.
- Colors are set with `--toast-color-*` CSS custom properties in your own CSS. The `tokens` and `nonce` options and the `ToastTokens` type are removed, and the package injects no `<style>` element, so a strict `style-src` policy needs no nonce.

## Fixed

- Dismissing a queued dialog no longer moves the toasts out of the dialog that is still open.
- Submitting a prompt with Enter no longer activates the element that opened it when focus returns there.
- A dialog whose element was removed, or whose `body` was replaced, is recreated instead of every later dialog failing.
- An update that only changes a toast's text keeps its action and dismiss buttons, so focus on them is kept.
- A dismissed toast restores focus only when its removal lost it, not when focus moved elsewhere during the exit animation.
- An update from an `onShow` subscriber no longer renders the content twice.
- `destroy()` after `clear()` finishes leaving toasts immediately, and a toast dismissed during its entrance animation can still have its exit cancelled.

<!-- Source: docs/changelog/0.3.1.md -->

# 0.3.1

## Changed

- Nothing a consumer imports has changed: the bundle is byte-identical to 0.3.0's, so upgrading needs no action. The release records its size for each export imported alone, and its bytes by source file, function, and class member, for the package index to show where they go.

<!-- Source: docs/changelog/0.3.0.md -->

# 0.3.0

## Added

- `labels.notifications` names each toast stack, which is now a region landmark that screen reader users can jump to.
- Dialog handles are exported as `DialogHandle`.

## Changed

- Screen readers hear toasts through hidden polite and assertive live regions that exist before any toast text, instead of through the toast element. Toast elements no longer carry `role` or `aria-live`; code or tests that query toasts by those attributes need another selector, such as `.coden-toast`.
- An actionable toast's announcement includes its action label.
- While a toaster's dialog is open, that toaster's toast stacks move inside the dialog, so they stay above the backdrop, clickable, and announced. Toasts from other toaster instances are not announced while it is open.
- `InteractiveToastHandle` is renamed `DialogHandle`.
- `PromiseToastOptions.loading` is typed `string | LoadingToastOptions`. Toast-only fields such as `duration` no longer type-check there; set them on the call's other options.
- An explicit `undefined` in toast options, `configure`, or dialog options is ignored instead of erasing the default. `configure({ tokens: undefined })` clears the instance's tokens.
- `toast.promise` applies the call's options and the `semantic` defaults to its success and error toasts.
